quote: und da sieht man, dass man zuvor die [-Zg-] 1- und die 2-gliedrige alle aufstellen muss.
english: And then one sees that one must first determine all the 1- and 2-parameter ones.
topic: Remarks on models as ends in themselves (citing Fritz Kötter's polemic against Klein–Sommerfeld on numerical computation), an analogy between the quadratic reciprocity law and hydraulic formulas, and a reflection that all thinking consists in finding simpler problems, illustrated by the parallel axiom and the determination of 3-parameter continuous transformation groups.

triage.modern_statement: This isn't really a research question. It's an example Hilbert uses to make a point about method: thinking means reducing a problem to simpler ones. The example is the problem of classifying all 3-parameter continuous (Lie) transformation groups, for instance local Lie group actions on the plane or, abstractly, real or complex 3-dimensional Lie algebras. To solve it, you first classify the 1- and 2-parameter groups, which appear as subgroups. That step was already the standard approach in Sophus Lie's classification work.
triage.answered_by: The underlying classification was done before this note. Sophus Lie classified the finite-dimensional Lie algebras of vector fields on the plane (local, over R and C) in his 1880s work on transformation groups. Luigi Bianchi classified the real 3-dimensional Lie algebras in 1898 (Memorie Soc. Ital. Sci., Ser. 3, vol. 11, pp. 267–352).

evidence.claim: Sophus Lie obtained the local classification of all Lie algebras of vector fields on the plane, over both R and C.
The Bianchi classification lists all real 3-dimensional Lie algebras up to isomorphism.
Bianchi published this classification in 1898 in 'Sugli spazi a tre dimensioni che ammettono un gruppo continuo di movimenti', Mem. Soc. Ital. Sci. Ser. 3, 11, 267.
Bianchi's 1898 result classifies three-dimensional Lie algebras and shows that every one has the same structure as an algebra on his list.

triage.why: The page is about how people think: you find simpler problems first. The 3-parameter group example illustrates that point and isn't posed as an open question. Its content, building the 3-parameter classification from the 1- and 2-parameter cases, matches Lie's existing method, and his classification (later Bianchi's 1898 list of real 3-dimensional Lie algebras) was already in print or followed soon after. It isn't among Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem. Fifth-problem connections are not mentioned in any source I found. The note is undated, so whether it came before or after Bianchi's paper is unclear, and that is why confidence is medium. None of the sources cited mention this note itself, so linking it to Lie's method and Bianchi's paper is my own reading.
